newsitem.title: UK: UK manufacturing output likely to rebound in June.
newsitem.headline: UK manufacturing output likely to rebound in June.

text.p: British manufacturing output is expected to stage a bounce-back in June after an unexpected fall in May, economists said.

The Reuters consensus forecast is for manufacturing output to grow 0.4 percent in June from the previous month and 1.2 percent year on year, while overall industrial production is likely to show increases of 0.5 percent and 1.2 percent respectively. The figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Tuesday.
Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers said the 1.1 percent month-on-month fall in May manufacturing output was due partly to a seven percent fall in car output, which had been reversed in June.

"Business surveys suggest that second-quarter manufacturing output continued to rise steadily and hence we expect that any erratic weakness in May's figures will also reverse in June," he wrote in his Sterling Weekly.
Saunders forecasts an above-consensus 1.0 percent monthly rise in June output and an 0.7 percent rise in overall production.
The July PMI manufacturing survey, published on August 1, showed manufacturing growing for the 14th month in a row despite a sharp fall in export demand.

Philip Shaw, chief economist at Investec, said he doubted that May's weakness signalled the start of a period of extended weakness in manufacturing, even though surveys showed export orders were suffering.

"Domestic demand appears to be making up the shortfall," he said. Shaw noted that when releasing preliminary second-quarter GDP estimates last week, the Office for National Statistics hinted that manufacturing output was broadly unchanged over the quarter.

"This would imply a modest recovery in June and our forecast of a 0.4 percent rise is consistent with this," he said. "However, we are at pains to point out that although May's fall clearly overstates the weakness in the sector, the current trend is little better than flat and there is a very real prospect that manufacturing will begin to fall again later this year as the level of the currency begins to bite."
Economists at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, by contrast, remain convinced that manufacturing will continue to record modest growth, despite concerns that it could face a sterling-led recession in 1998.
"Although the export side is weakening rapidly, domestic demand is robust enough to compensate at present," they wrote in their weekly look-ahead.
Simon Bowmaker of HSBC expects a rebound in June oil and gas output and says energy supply is also likely to have been greater due to the month's poor weather.
"Overall, we expect total output to rise by a stronger 0.7 percent in June, with the annual rate increasing to 1.4 percent." he said.
